title: Euler's Polyhedron Formula
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: For any convex polyhedron, vertices minus edges plus faces always equals 2.
short: Count corners, subtract edges, add faces: for a sphere-shaped solid the answer is always two.
long: Euler noticed that this alternating count is a topological invariant: stretching or bending the polyhedron leaves it unchanged. It fails for a torus-shaped polyhedron, where the count is 0 instead. The number 2 is the Euler characteristic of the sphere, so the formula is really a statement about shape, not about straight edges or flat faces.
proof: Project the graph to a plane; deleting an edge shared by two faces reduces E and F by one and leaves V-E+F unchanged. Repeat until a spanning tree remains, where E=V-1 and F=1, giving V-E+F=2.
consequence: It limits the Platonic solids to five, motivates the Euler characteristic, and is the prototype for counting invariants in topology.

title: The Gauss–Bonnet Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: For a compact surface with boundary, total Gaussian curvature plus total boundary geodesic curvature equals 2π times the Euler characteristic.
short: A surface's total bending is dictated by its topology: sphere, torus and cylinder cannot share the same total curvature.
long: On a closed surface the boundary term vanishes, so the total Gaussian curvature is 2π times the Euler characteristic: a sphere must have total curvature 4π, while a torus has total curvature zero. The theorem converts a local, metric quantity into a global integer, and it holds for every Riemannian metric on the surface. It is the prototype for index theorems in higher dimensions.
proof: Triangulate by geodesic arcs; a geodesic polygon satisfies ∫K + sum of exterior angles = 2π. Summing over the triangulation, interior edges cancel and the angle defects add to 2πχ(M) by Euler's formula.
consequence: It explains why a torus can carry a flat metric but a sphere cannot, and it opens the door to the Chern–Gauss–Bonnet theorem and higher index theorems.

title: The Hairy Ball Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: On an even-dimensional sphere, every continuous tangent vector field vanishes somewhere — you cannot comb a hairy ball flat.
short: Any tangential flow on a sphere must have a stagnation point: there is no way to point a nonzero arrow at every point.
long: Wind blowing tangentially over a spherical planet must be still somewhere. Equivalently, S^n admits a nowhere-vanishing tangent field exactly when n is odd, so S^2 fails while S^3 succeeds. The obstruction is the Euler class: on S^2 it evaluates to the Euler characteristic 2, which rules out a nonvanishing field.
proof: A nowhere-zero tangent field normalises to a unit field u. Then H(x,t)=cos(πt)x+sin(πt)u(x) joins the identity map of S^n (degree 1) to the antipodal map (degree (−1)^{n+1}=−1 for even n), which is impossible.
consequence: It forces calm points in tangential flows, explains why even-dimensional spheres are not parallelisable, and links vector fields to characteristic classes.

title: The Borsuk–Ulam Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Every continuous map from an n-sphere to n-dimensional space takes the same value at some antipodal pair of points.
short: Any continuous labelling of opposite directions with n numbers must agree somewhere on a diametrically opposite pair.
long: For a continuous assignment of n real numbers to each direction on an n-sphere, some pair of opposite directions receives exactly the same vector. The statement is equivalent to saying that no continuous odd map S^n→S^{n−1} exists. Its proof uses mod-2 homology, which makes it a close cousin of the fixed-point theorems.
proof: If f(x)≠f(−x) everywhere, then g(x)=f(x)−f(−x) is odd and nonzero, so g/|g|:S^n→S^{n−1} is odd. An odd map induces the nonzero identity on H_n(ℝP^n;ℤ/2), but H_n(ℝP^{n−1};ℤ/2)=0 — contradiction.
consequence: It yields the ham sandwich theorem, fair-division results, Lovász's proof of the Kneser conjecture, and lower bounds in topology-driven combinatorics.

title: The Jordan Curve Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: A simple closed curve in the plane splits it into exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, with the curve as their common boundary.
short: Every non-self-intersecting loop has a definite inside and outside, even when the curve is wildly irregular.
long: The claim looks obvious for a circle but is surprisingly hard for a general continuous loop, because the curve need not be smooth or rectifiable. The theorem guarantees exactly two complementary components and that the curve is the boundary of each. Its higher-dimensional analogue, the Jordan–Brouwer separation theorem, fails for some wild embeddings.
proof: For a polygonal loop, a ray from a point crosses the curve an even or odd number of times, separating inside from outside; general curves follow by approximation. Alexander duality gives reduced H_0(ℝ²∖J) = reduced H^1(J) = ℤ, so there are exactly two components.
consequence: It makes inside and outside rigorous, underlies planar graph embeddings and the Schönflies problem, and models separation results in higher dimensions.

title: The Poincaré Conjecture
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: A closed three-manifold in which every loop can be shrunk to a point is homeomorphic to the 3-sphere.
short: Among closed 3-dimensional spaces, simple connectivity characterises the 3-sphere — a claim that took a century to prove.
long: Poincaré asked in 1904 whether a closed 3-manifold with trivial fundamental group must be the 3-sphere; the higher-dimensional cases were settled decades earlier. Grigori Perelman proved the three-dimensional case in 2002–03 using Ricci flow with surgery, building on Richard Hamilton's programme. The result is the centrepiece of Thurston's geometrisation conjecture.
proof: Hamilton's Ricci flow smooths a metric by a heat-type equation; Perelman's entropy monotonicity and surgery control the singularities. For a simply connected closed 3-manifold the flow becomes a round sphere in finite time.
consequence: Together with geometrisation it completes the structural classification of closed 3-manifolds and reshaped modern topology.

title: Classification of Compact Surfaces
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Every closed connected surface is a sphere, a connected sum of tori, or a connected sum of real projective planes.
short: Two pieces of data — orientability and genus — determine a closed surface completely up to homeomorphism.
long: The orientable list is the sphere, the torus, the double torus and so on; the non-orientable list begins with the real projective plane and the Klein bottle. Because Euler characteristic is 2−2g in the orientable case and 2−k in the non-orientable case, orientability plus Euler characteristic is a complete invariant. Every closed surface therefore has one of these normal forms.
proof: Triangulate and cut along arcs until a polygon with paired edges remains; simplifying the edge word yields ∏[a_i,b_i] (orientable) or ∏ c_i² (non-orientable), the connected-sum normal forms.
consequence: It reduces the study of closed surfaces to two integer invariants and organises questions about maps, coverings and moduli.

title: The Möbius Strip
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Gluing a rectangle's ends with a half-twist gives one side and one boundary circle; a loop around it swaps left and right.
short: A single half-twist fuses the two sides of a strip into one and its two boundary edges into a single circle.
long: Give a strip of paper one half-twist and tape the ends: the two original sides join into one. The boundary is a single circle, and walking once around returns you to the starting place on the opposite apparent side. Cutting along the centre line produces one longer band, not two separate bands.
proof: The two short edges of the rectangle are glued in opposite directions, so its two long edges form a single circle. A loop around the core reverses a local normal vector, so no continuous choice of side exists; its double cover is a cylinder.
consequence: It is the simplest non-orientable surface; capping its boundary with a disc gives the real projective plane, and it recurs in topology, chemistry and art.

title: The Banach–Tarski Paradox
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: A solid ball can be cut into finitely many pieces and reassembled into two solid balls of the same size.
latex: B^3\ \sim\ B^3\sqcup B^3\quad(\text{finitely many pieces, rotations only})
short: With non-measurable pieces and the axiom of choice, volume is no longer preserved by dissection.
long: The pieces are not measurable, so there is no volume to conserve: additivity applies only to measurable sets. The construction uses a free subgroup of rotations of the sphere and the axiom of choice to pick orbit representatives; without choice the argument collapses. No analogous paradox exists in the plane using rotations and translations.
proof: SO(3) contains a free group on two generators. Its action on S² lets one split the sphere into finitely many orbit-representative pieces that reassemble into two copies; extending radially and absorbing the centre gives two balls.
consequence: It shows why measure theory must restrict to sigma-algebras and led to the notion of amenable groups in geometric group theory.

title: The Four Colour Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Any planar map can be coloured with four colours so that regions sharing a border segment get different colours.
short: Five colours are easy; four required a century of work and the first famous computer-assisted proof.
long: Equivalently, every planar graph has chromatic number at most 4. Regions touching only at a single point may share a colour. Appel and Haken proved the result in 1977 by checking a finite list of unavoidable configurations; later work shortened the check and produced a formal verification.
proof: Reduce to a maximal planar triangulation. Any minimal counterexample must contain one of finitely many unavoidable configurations, each of which is reducible; checking that finite list by computer rules out the counterexample.
consequence: It stimulated computer-assisted and formally verified mathematics and remains a benchmark for planar graph algorithms.

title: Desargues' Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Two triangles perspective from a point are perspective from a line: their three corresponding side-intersections are collinear.
short: A central projection of one triangle onto another automatically aligns three crossed side-intersections.
long: If the lines joining corresponding vertices pass through one point, then the intersections of corresponding sides lie on one line, and conversely. The theorem holds in every projective space of dimension at least two over a field, but in abstract projective planes it must be assumed as an axiom. Its failure marks the exotic non-Desarguesian planes.
proof: Lift the two triangles into distinct planes through the perspectivity centre; corresponding sides meet in both planes, hence on their common line. Projecting back gives the planar result; homogeneous coordinates give an algebraic proof.
consequence: It is a foundational theorem of projective geometry and separates Desarguesian planes from non-Desarguesian ones.

title: Pappus's Hexagon Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Six points alternating on two lines produce three cross-intersections that always lie on one straight line.
short: A hidden straight line emerges from six dots on two lines — one of the oldest projective theorems.
long: Take A, B, C on one line and A', B', C' on another. Cross-connecting the triples gives three intersection points, and Pappus says they are collinear. In the axiomatic development of projective geometry this incidence theorem is equivalent to commutativity of the coordinate field.
proof: Choose coordinates making the two lines the axes, write A=(a,0), A'=(0,a') and so on, then compute the three intersections; they satisfy a single linear equation.
consequence: It underpins the synthetic characterisation of projective spaces over fields and gives a classical source of incidence theorems.

title: The Ham Sandwich Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: In n dimensions, any n measurable bodies can be bisected at once by a single hyperplane.
short: One straight cut can halve the bread, the cheese and the ham simultaneously.
long: For three bounded measurable objects in space there is a plane that halves all three by volume. The result extends to n bodies in n dimensions and has discrete versions for finite point sets, where the cut must split each set as evenly as possible. It is a direct consequence of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem.
proof: For a normal direction u, let f_i(u) be the signed difference of the two half-space measures of body i; f:S^n→ℝ^n is continuous and odd. Borsuk–Ulam gives f(u)=f(−u), and oddness gives f(−u)=−f(u), hence f(u)=0.
consequence: It is a classic fair-division tool and drives algorithms for simultaneous partitions in computational geometry.

title: Pick's Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: For a lattice polygon, area equals interior lattice points plus half the boundary lattice points minus one.
short: You can measure a lattice polygon just by counting the dots on and inside it.
long: Pick's theorem applies to simple polygons whose vertices have integer coordinates. It converts a continuous quantity, area, into two discrete counts, and it has no direct analogue for polyhedra in three dimensions. The formula is exact, not an approximation, for every such polygon.
proof: Both sides are additive when a polygon is cut into lattice triangles. Verify the formula directly for a lattice rectangle and a right lattice triangle (or its complement in one), then triangulate any lattice polygon.
consequence: It opens the theory of Ehrhart polynomials, which count lattice points in dilates of polytopes, and links the geometry of numbers to combinatorics.
